theater: 卡累利阿地峽與曼納海姆防線

battle.name: 冬季戰爭
battle.theater: 卡累利阿地峽與曼納海姆防線
battle.brief: 一九三九年十一月三十日蘇聯進攻芬蘭，四〇年三月十三日停戰，歷時一百零五天。芬軍退守卡累利阿地峽的曼納海姆防線死守數月，又以滑雪兵在森林中分割包抄，擊潰蘇軍數個縱隊。卡面的索米衝鋒槍 KP/-31 配發步兵班與民兵，專司工事近戰、雪地夜襲與反突擊。

kit.name: 索米衝鋒槍
kit.history: 1931年列裝後，索米衝鋒槍成為芬蘭步兵的主要近戰武器，冬季戰爭期間廣泛配屬於步兵班與滑雪兵，用於近距離火力。

countries: 冬季戰爭的交戰雙方是芬蘭與蘇聯。芬蘭方面的最高決策機構是國防委員會，由內閣、國防部與國會代表組成；一九三九年十一月二十六日國會以壓倒多數通過應戰決議，授權政府總動員，芬蘭遂在對方未宣戰的情況下應戰。實際作戰由最高指揮官曼納海姆元帥統轄，總參謀長則在戰事爆發當日由奧斯泰爾曼將軍交給奧埃什將軍。芬軍野戰部隊約三十萬至三十四萬人，由十二個師擴編為十六個師另加旅團，編成南部地峽集團軍（曼納海姆直接指揮）、北部集團軍（奧埃什）與拉普蘭集團軍；國民警衛隊另有約三十萬人，負責就地防衛、後方城鎮與補充線，並有數萬名自願參戰者補入各營。編制上，芬軍步兵師約一萬四千五百人，師轄三團、團轄三營、營轄四排，每排約三十人；蘇軍步兵師約八千至一萬二千人，兵力較小但排的火力密度更高，裝備與自動武器比例較大。蘇聯一側由九月成立的戰爭特別委員會統籌，主席先後為伏羅希洛夫與元月接手的鐵木真哥；其作戰序列為面向地峽的第四軍（梅列茨科夫）、攻入東卡累利阿的第十六軍（戈利科夫）、打通北翼的第十三軍（卡扎科夫）與總預備的第三軍，合計二十一至二十六個步兵師，其中近半是剛完成改編、冬季裝備不足的新建師。蘇方參戰兵力在四十五萬至七十六萬之間（蘇方另宣稱逾百萬），空軍逾一千架、戰車數百輛。雙方的地理條件同樣懸殊：蘇聯可自北、中、南三個方向同時壓上，芬蘭的國土南北狹長，主要防線只集中在卡累利阿地峽一線，其後便是首都與工業區所在的南部。情報落差亦相明顯：蘇方情報機構明知芬蘭境內正在構築堡壘，仍低估其強度；芬方則在開戰前已掌握蘇軍沿鐵路向北集結的跡象。整體而言，芬蘭是以數量劣勢的步兵、滑雪兵與為數不多的自動武器，靠堡壘體系、森林地形與嚴寒氣候抵禦蘇軍的機械化優勢。
countriesEn: The Winter War was fought between Finland and the Soviet Union. On the Finnish side the highest decision-making body was the Defence Council, composed of the cabinet, the defence ministry and parliamentary representatives; on 26 November 1939 the parliament approved a declaration of war by an overwhelming majority and authorised the government to mobilise, and Finland thus went to war without having received a formal declaration from the other side. Operations were run by the Supreme Commander, Marshal Mannerheim, while the Chief of the General Staff changed hands on the very first day of the war, from General Österman to General Oesch. Finland's field army numbered roughly 300,000 to 340,000 men, expanded from twelve divisions to sixteen divisions plus brigades, and was organised into the Army of the Isthmus under Mannerheim's own command, the North Finland Group under Oesch, and the Lapland Group; the Home Guard added some 300,000 men responsible for local defence, the rear towns and the lines of communication, and tens of thousands of volunteers were folded into the battalions. In terms of organisation, the Finnish infantry division numbered about 14,500 men in three regiments, three battalions to a regiment and four platoons to a battalion, each platoon of roughly thirty men; Soviet rifle divisions numbered between 8,000 and 12,000, smaller formations with denser firepower per man and a higher proportion of equipment and automatic weapons. On the Soviet side the campaign was directed by a special committee created in September 1939, chaired first by Voroshilov and from January by Timoshenko. The Soviet order of battle comprised the Fourth Army (Meretskov) facing the Karelian Isthmus, the Sixteenth Army (Golikov) operating in East Karelia, the Thirteenth Army (Kazakov) fighting at Salla, and the Third Army held in general reserve, some twenty-one to twenty-six rifle divisions in all, nearly half of them newly formed divisions reorganised only shortly before the war and short of winter equipment. Estimates of Soviet strength range from 450,000 to 760,000 men (Moscow claimed over a million), with more than a thousand aircraft and several hundred tanks. The geographical imbalance was just as stark: the Soviet Union could press in from three directions at once, whereas Finland was long and narrow, and its principal defensive line lay only on the Karelian Isthmus, with the capital and the industrial south immediately behind it. Intelligence was no better balanced: Soviet intelligence knew that fortifications were being built in Finland yet still underestimated their strength, while the Finns had already picked up signs of Soviet concentrations moving north by rail before the war began. In strategic terms Finland fought a numerically inferior force of infantry and ski troops, backed by only a small number of automatic weapons, and relied on field fortifications, forest terrain and severe frost to offset the Soviet weight of metal.
people: 曼納海姆在冬季戰爭中由國防委員會主席升任最高指揮官，並於一九三九年十二月二十日受封元帥；他開戰當日正在卡累利阿地峽前線視察堡壘工程，蘇軍開火時他就在前線，這段經歷成為其戰役日誌與事後回憶中最常被引用的部分，亦是本戰最重要的史料之一。總參謀長奧埃什接手整體策劃，參謀本部則由工程出身的埃里克·海因里希斯以少將身份率第三軍，即後來人所稱的S集群，在索馬斯阿爾米與拉阿特公路作戰；海因里希斯主持的戰鬥研究處同時推出「火力分配表」（tulokasvi），把分散的輕重機槍與砲兵按統一射表分配射界，被視為曼納海姆防線得以長期固守的技術關鍵。希拉普西亞在西線的拉阿特公路反擊中指揮S集群，翌年一月的伊洛曼齊又以第十四師圍殲蘇軍兩個師；帕亞里以第三師在托爾瓦耶爾維擊敗蘇軍第一百三十九師，後來在塔利－伊杭塔拉以第六師頂住突破。蘇聯方面，梅列茨科夫的第四軍是最後攻破曼納海姆防線者，戈利科夫在東卡累利阿屢攻不下，卡扎科夫在薩拉打通了北翼；元月起接手特別委員會的鐵木真哥與參謀總部的朱可夫，則以新戰法替蘇軍挽回頹勢。芬蘭總統里沃·尤霍·基尤科主持民政後方與受戰火波及區的安置，外交部長魯道夫·霍爾斯蒂同莫斯科周旋；蘇方對芬的最後通牒由外交人民委員莫洛托夫發出。雙方的情報首腦同樣關鍵：芬蘭軍事情報處長瓦爾托寧的邊境報告被視為開戰前的重要預警，而蘇聯軍事情報機構雖然察覺芬蘭正大舉築壘，報告卻被壓下，沒有反映到作戰計畫之中。參謀本部與最高指揮官之間亦有張力：曼納海姆數度希望在北部更早更狠地反擊，參謀長奧埃什與海因里希斯則主張先用滑雪游擊消磨敵縱隊，待其拉長後再行分割，兩種指揮風格在同一條防線上互相補位，最終合成以守待攻再反擊的獨特打法。
peopleEn: Mannerheim rose from chairman of the Defence Council to Supreme Commander during the Winter War and was raised to the rank of marshal on 20 December 1939. On the day the war began he was inspecting the fortification works on the Karelian Isthmus, and the Soviet guns opened while he was at the front; that experience became the most frequently quoted part of his war diary and later recollections, and his writings remain the single most important body of source material for the conflict. General Oesch took over as Chief of the General Staff and the overall planning of operations. Erik Heinrichs, an engineer by training, commanded the III Corps, the improvised Group S, at Suomussalmi and along the Raate road; the combat research office he headed at the same time produced the fire distribution table (tulokasvi), which allotted sectors of fire to scattered light and heavy machine guns and artillery under a single firing plan, and is regarded as the technical key to the long endurance of the Mannerheim Line. Siilasvuo commanded Group S during the counter-attack on the Raate road, and in January 1940 his 14th Division encircled two Soviet divisions at Ilomantsi. Pajari defeated the Soviet 139th Rifle Division at Tolvajärvi with his 3rd Division and later held the breach at Tali-Ihantala with the 6th. On the Soviet side Meretskov's Fourth Army was the formation that finally broke the Mannerheim Line, Golikov failed repeatedly in East Karelia, and Kazakov opened the northern flank at Salla; from January Timoshenko, who took over the special committee, and Zhukov in the General Staff began to pull the Soviet campaign back together with new methods. Finland's president Kyösti Kallio handled civilian administration and the resettlement of the districts struck by war, while the foreign minister Rudolf Holsti carried on the negotiations with Moscow; the Soviet ultimatum to Finland was read out by the People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs, Molotov, on 26 November 1939. The intelligence chiefs on both sides mattered just as much: reports from the Finnish military intelligence chief, Valtonen, were treated as a significant pre-war warning, and although Soviet intelligence detected the great Finnish construction effort, the reports were suppressed and never reached the operational plans. There was also tension between the general staff and the supreme commander: Mannerheim several times wanted a harder and earlier counter-attack in the north, whereas Oesch and Heinrichs argued for wearing down the enemy columns with ski raiding first and cutting them up only once they had stretched. The two styles of command complemented one another on the same defensive line and together produced the distinctive Finnish method of waiting and then counter-attacking.
kits: 卡面的索米衝鋒槍KP/-31是芬蘭自製的一代戰後武器：口徑七六二乘二五公釐手槍彈，直彈匣二十發，另有三十六發與五十發的長彈匣；機身以鋼片沖壓成型，配可折合木槍托與片狀散熱式槍口防焰器，循環射速約每分鐘四百五十發，全重約三點五公斤，有效射程在一百至二百公尺之間，瞄具為固定的缺口照門與准星，槍口初速約四百公尺。一九三一年列裝後，它主要配發步兵班班長、滑雪兵與國民警衛隊，負責接近戰、固守工事、反突擊與村屋地帶的近身交火，是芬軍在輕機槍不足時的重要補充火力；冬季戰爭中它在林線、村屋與碉堡反衝鋒的場面尤其常見。芬軍的骨幹仍然是莫辛－納甘步槍（不少是繳獲的蘇軍莫辛與SVT）與拉蒂－薩洛蘭塔M/26、馬克西姆M/32/39輕機槍，反裝甲則靠拉蒂L-39反器材步槍、七六公釐連隊砲與臨時炸藥瓶；蘇軍以T-26與BT-5輕型戰車、七六公釐師屬砲、四十五公釐反戰車砲投入，二月突破時更調入KV-1重型戰車與大量牽引砲，並以一五二公釐榴彈砲反覆轟擊堡壘頂部。芬軍在戰中繳獲蘇軍步槍逾十萬支、機槍數千挺、輕砲數百門與數十輛戰車（各書數字不一），並用這些裝備武裝民兵與新組建的營，連同雪鞋、滑雪板與白色偽裝用布，都靠冬季作戰的實戰經驗補足。空軍方面，芬蘭的主力是三十架法製莫蘭－索爾尼耶MS.406與瑞典贈送的颶風式戰鬥機，另有向波蘭購入的戰鬥機與一批老舊機型；蘇聯空軍以逾千架的絕對優勢掩護地峽進攻，幾乎每日都掌握制空權。湖上與海上亦有對手：芬蘭在維堡灣與拉多加湖以岸上重砲與湖上砲艇支援陸戰，蘇聯的戰列艦與巡洋艦則在波羅的海以艦炮支援地面攻勢並攔截海上運輸。
kitsEn: The submachine gun on the card, the KP/-31, was a home-grown Finnish weapon of the interwar period. It fired 7.62 x 25 mm pistol ammunition from a twenty-round straight magazine, with 36-round and 50-round extended magazines also produced. The receiver was stamped from sheet steel, and the weapon carried a folding wooden stock and a finned flash hider, a cyclic rate of fire of roughly 450 rounds per minute, a weight of about 3.5 kg, an effective range of between 100 and 200 metres with fixed aperture sights, and a muzzle velocity of roughly 400 m/s. Once adopted in 1931 it was issued mainly to section leaders, ski troops and the Home Guard, and its jobs were close combat, the defence of positions, counter-attacks and fighting in village houses, making it the principal supplement to Finnish firepower where light machine guns were too few; in the Winter War it appears most often in the treeline, in village houses and in the counter-attack against captured bunkers. The backbone of the Finnish infantry remained the Mosin-Nagant rifle, many of them captured Soviet Mosins and SVTs, together with the Lahti-Saloranta M/26 and Maxim M/32-39 light machine guns, while anti-armour work was done with the Lahti L-39 anti-tank rifle, 76 mm regimental guns and improvised bottles of incendiary mixture. The Soviet army committed T-26 and BT-5 light tanks, 76 mm divisional guns and 45 mm anti-tank guns, and during the February breakthrough added KV-1 heavy tanks and large numbers of towed artillery, repeatedly shelling the concrete roofs of the bunkers with 152 mm howitzers. Finnish forces captured from the Red Army during the war more than 100,000 rifles, several thousand machine guns, several hundred light guns and a few dozen tanks, with the published figures differing, and armed the Home Guard and newly raised battalions with them; snowshoes, skis and white camouflage cloth were likewise improvised out of the lessons of real winter fighting. In the air, the Finnish force centred on thirty French Morane-Saulnier MS.406 fighters and the Hawker Hurricanes donated by Sweden, together with fighters bought from Poland and a batch of obsolete types; the Soviet air force, with an absolute numerical advantage of more than a thousand machines, supported the offensive on the Isthmus and held the air almost every day. There were opponents on the lakes and at sea as well: the Finnish coastal artillery and lake gunboats supported the land battle in the Gulf of Vyborg and on Lake Ladoga, while Soviet battleships and cruisers shelled from the Baltic in support of the ground offensive and interdicted coastal traffic.
tactics: 冬季戰爭的戰術核心是「以森林與堡壘拖住、以滑雪兵切斷」。北線蘇軍以細長縱隊沿公路挺進，縱隊在公路上首尾相接數公里，車隊之間缺乏掩護，結果在拉阿特公路被芬軍以滑雪兵側擊、首尾切斷，再用「莫蒂」（motti，伐木場包圍）方式逐段殲滅，蘇軍第44與第163步兵師正是這樣在零下三十度的雪地裡散架：縱隊被切開後，車輛因引擎凍僵與燃料耗盡而原地癱瘓，後續部隊只能在一片白茫中重蹈覆轍。芬軍的辦法是先把敵隊縱隊分隔成數段，再用小隊逐一殲滅，攻擊時以白色偽裝接近，再集中火力打擊其側後。南線芬軍退入曼納海姆防線：以約一百三十五公里的混凝土堡壘群構成兩至三道防線，配置交通壕、反戰車壕、鐵刺網與地雷，堡壘之間以重機槍與輕機槍的交叉火力互相支援，並以統一火力分配表協調砲兵射界——每個目標都有專責的射擊單位與備射安排，任何一點遭到攻擊，相鄰堡壘立即補射；冬天則靠滑雪兵在林間巡邏封鎖夜間接近，車輛用白帆布覆蓋以免在雪地上反光。蘇軍在二月的突破倚仗集中砲兵與戰車群，以密集火力先壓制堡壘射孔，再讓步兵沿彈坑與地形接近；突破正面狹窄，數公里的堡壘線上同時只有數個師投入。芬軍在塔利－伊杭塔拉等路口死守，等待蘇軍縱隊拉長後再以側擊與分割重演北線的殲滅法，其代價是維堡方向的曼納海姆最終下令放棄，並在三月十九日當選總統。整條補給線是蘇軍的致命弱點：連接列寧格勒與前線的單線鐵路與公路每日運力有限，冬季裝備不足，前線部隊到一、二月才陸續收到棉衣與裝備，而燃料與飼料的缺口令許多縱隊在出發前就已耗盡體力。三月一日至三日的武奧薩爾米一役最能說明此法：蘇軍縱隊在維堡公路上被芬軍以路障與兩翼火力逐段吃掉，武奧薩爾米車站一帶的戰鬥持續整整三日，芬軍在沒有時間建立縱深的情況下仍把蘇軍一個師打殘；三月十日至十一日的伊杭塔拉一役則是芬軍防禦的極限，此後便再無反攻的本錢。
tacticsEn: The tactical core of the Winter War was to hold with forests and fortifications and to cut with ski troops. In the north the Soviet army advanced in long narrow columns along the roads, trains stretching for several kilometres with little cover between vehicles, and the columns were then hit from the flank by Finnish ski troops, cut front and rear, and destroyed section by section using what the Finns called the motti, a logging-camp blockade. The Soviet 44th and 163rd Rifle Divisions disintegrated in exactly this fashion in thirty-degree cold: once a column was severed, its vehicles froze solid or ran out of fuel and stalled on the spot, and the units that followed ploughed into the same white emptiness. The Finnish method was to divide the enemy column into segments first and then annihilate each segment in turn, approaching in white camouflage and concentrating fire on the flanks and rear. In the south the Finnish army fell back onto the Mannerheim Line, a chain of concrete bunkers running some 135 kilometres in two or three lines, with communication trenches, anti-tank ditches, steel chevaux-de-frise and minefields, mutually supporting crossfire from heavy and light machine guns, and artillery fire coordinated through the same fire distribution tables: every target had a dedicated firing unit and a standby arrangement, so that the moment one position was attacked, the neighbouring bunkers opened fire in support. In winter ski patrols in the woods sealed off approaches by night, and vehicles were covered with white canvas so that they would not throw back light against the snow. The February Soviet breakthrough relied on massed artillery and tank groups, which first suppressed the bunker embrasures with concentrated fire before infantry advanced along shell craters and broken ground; the front was narrow, and at any moment only a few divisions were committed across a few kilometres of the bunker line. The Finns held firm at road junctions such as Tali-Ihantala, waited for the Soviet columns to stretch, and then repeated the northern pattern of flank attacks and encirclement, at the price of Mannerheim's decision to abandon Vyborg, and of his election as president on 19 March. Supply was the fatal weakness of the Soviet offensive: the single-track railway and the roads linking Leningrad to the front could carry only so much each day, winter clothing was short, and the troops in the line did not begin to receive greatcoats and equipment in quantity until January and February, while shortages of fuel and fodder drained the columns before they even set off. The fighting at Vuosalmi from 1 to 3 March illustrates the method best: Soviet columns on the Vyborg road were cut up piece by piece by roadblocks and flanking fire, the battle around the Vuosalmi station lasted three full days, and the Finns destroyed much of a Soviet division even without time to build a depth; the clash at Ihantala on 10 and 11 March was the limit of Finnish defence, after which there were no reserves left for counter-attacking.
data: 可核對的數字集中在幾處。戰事自一九三九年十一月三十日至四〇年三月十三日，前後一百零五天。芬軍野戰部隊約三十萬至三十四萬人，國民警衛隊另有約三十萬，蘇軍投入二十一至二十六個步兵師、四十五萬至七十六萬人，空軍逾一千架、戰車數百輛。曼納海姆防線全長約一百三十五公里，堡壘逾三百五十座、散兵坑約一千七百八十五個，耗用混凝土約二萬八千噸、鋼材約四千噸，據守兵力約九萬；蘇軍二月的突破正面狹窄，主要突破點只佔數公里。芬蘭空軍開戰時只有一百一十四架作戰機，到四〇年三月增至約三百二十架，常見引述係空軍自身損失僅得個位數機、而擊落蘇機逾一百架（各書統計不一）。芬軍官方公佈陣亡約二萬五千九百人、負傷約四萬三千六百人；蘇軍陣亡人數在十二萬至十七萬之間爭議，負傷與病患約二十六萬，冬季裝備不足造成的凍傷與病患是其中一大塊。戰後芬蘭按和約支付十四萬枚金幣的戰爭賠償，割地總面積約佔全國一成多，境內被迫遷移的卡累利阿居民數以萬計，被蘇軍佔領區的居民更被成批送往白海與西伯亞的勞動營地。此外，芬軍在戰爭期間繳獲的蘇軍裝備數量本身也是一項數據：步槍逾十萬支、機槍數千挺、輕砲數百門、卡車數百輛，數目雖各家不一，卻足以說明蘇軍縱隊在雪地裡連同車輛一併被收繳的規模。編制與距離亦可核對：芬軍步兵排約三十人，蘇軍排約八至十人，兩者兵力密度之比約三比一；冬季氣溫常在零下三十度以下，風雪令蘇軍車隊的行程往往比計畫慢上一倍；曼納海姆防線與維堡之間的縱深不過二三十公里，芬軍幾乎沒有可以退守的第二道陣地。
dataEn: The verifiable figures cluster in a few places. The war ran from 30 November 1939 to 13 March 1940, a hundred and five days. Finnish field forces numbered about 300,000 to 340,000 men, with the Home Guard contributing a further 300,000; the Soviet Union committed twenty-one to twenty-six rifle divisions and between 450,000 and 760,000 men, with more than a thousand aircraft and several hundred tanks. The Mannerheim Line ran for about 135 kilometres and contained over 350 bunkers and some 1,785 foxholes, consuming roughly 28,000 tonnes of concrete and 4,000 tonnes of steel, and was held by about 90,000 men. The February breakthrough front was narrow, with the main breach confined to a few kilometres. The Finnish Air Force owned only 114 combat aircraft at the outbreak of the war, rising to roughly 320 by March 1940, and it is commonly said that it lost only single-figure numbers of machines while shooting down more than a hundred Soviet aircraft, though the published counts differ. Official Finnish figures give 25,904 dead and 43,557 wounded; Soviet dead are put between 126,000 and 168,000 depending on the source, with around 264,000 wounded or sick, and a large share of the sickness was frostbite and exposure caused by the shortage of winter clothing. Under the peace terms Finland paid war reparations of 140,000 gold coins, ceded territory of roughly a tenth of the country, and saw tens of thousands of Karelians uprooted from their homes; the population of the occupied districts was deported in batches to labour camps around the White Sea and in Siberia. The quantity of Soviet equipment captured by the Finns is itself a figure worth stating: more than 100,000 rifles, several thousand machine guns, several hundred light guns and hundreds of trucks, whatever the exact counts, shows the scale at which Soviet columns were stripped in the snow, vehicles and all. Organisation and distances can also be checked: a Finnish infantry platoon held about thirty men against eight to ten in a Soviet platoon, a ratio of roughly three to one in density; winter temperatures commonly fell below thirty degrees below zero, and blizzards slowed Soviet convoys to half the planned rate; and the depth between the Mannerheim Line and Vyborg was no more than twenty or thirty kilometres, so the Finns had almost no second line to fall back on.
cause: 蘇聯在開戰前一年的外交布局已經收緊：一九三九年三月與德國簽訂互不侵犯條約，九月再以附加議定書瓜分波蘭，十月分別與愛沙尼亞、拉脫維亞簽訂互助條約，波羅的海沿岸自此盡入莫斯科的勢力範圍。芬蘭雖然在一九三八年與蘇聯簽訂互助條約，又向法國大量採購軍火，但莫斯科同時把幾項要求擺上桌面：解散芬蘭境內的共產黨組織、驅逐境內的波蘭人團體、租借北極圈內的佩察莫地區、以及放棄奧蘭群島的軍備限制。中蘇在北卡累利阿的邊界爭議、芬蘭與德國日益接近的跡象，加上芬蘭自波蘭購進的一批軍火在白海被蘇軍截獲、令莫斯科懷疑芬蘭已下定攻擊決心，令蘇聯相信芬蘭終會倒向西方。芬蘭自己則發現西方式的援手並不可靠：英法在慕尼黑協定之後對捷克的背棄，已經把互助條約的信譽損盡，指望中的援軍最終只來了數百名瑞典志願兵與一批物資。九月十七日蘇聯入侵波蘭之後，芬蘭國內要求自保的聲浪升高，莫斯科仍把芬蘭視為下一步目標，最終在沒有正式宣戰的情況下直接開火。國際聯盟在十二月將此案列為審議事項，一九四〇年三月發表的調查報告判定蘇聯的行動構成侵略，惟蘇聯早已被排除在聯盟的活動之外，制裁遂無從落實。德國因素同樣關鍵：三十年代後期德國與芬蘭有密切的經濟往來，鉀鹽與鎳礦的貿易讓德國取得北極圈的資源，而蘇聯視之為德國在芬蘭擴張勢力範圍的通道，一九三九年德國更與芬蘭簽訂秘密協議，蘇聯對此並非不知情。莫斯科同時亟需一場勝利，向西方證明其行動屬於防衛性質並鞏固東歐的新秩序；芬蘭內部亦有自己的考慮，國防委員會與總統府都不願見到共產黨在戰時坐大，而戰前芬蘭共產黨的影響力急升，這一點同樣列入莫斯科的算計。
causeEn: Soviet diplomatic preparations had been tightening for a full year before the shooting started. In March 1939 Moscow signed a non-aggression pact with Germany, in September it added a secret protocol dividing Poland, and in October it concluded treaties of mutual assistance with Estonia and Latvia, which left the whole Baltic littoral inside the Soviet sphere of influence. Finland had signed a treaty of friendship and cooperation with the Soviet Union in 1938 and ordered large quantities of arms from France, but Moscow at the same time pressed a list of demands on Helsinki: disbanding Communist organisations inside Finland, expelling the Polish group in the country, leasing the Arctic territory of Petsamo, and dropping the demilitarisation of the Åland Islands. Border disputes in North Karelia, the visible drift of Finland towards Germany, and the seizure by Soviet forces in the White Sea of a consignment of Polish arms bought by Finland, which convinced Moscow that Helsinki had already resolved to attack, all reinforced the belief that Finland would eventually turn to the West. The Finns discovered in turn that Western guarantees were unreliable: the abandonment of Czechoslovakia after the Munich Agreement had already destroyed the credibility of mutual assistance, and the foreign volunteers and supplies that actually arrived came to a few hundred Swedes and a modest shipment of materiel. After the Soviet invasion of Poland on 17 September, pressure inside Finland for armed self-defence rose, yet Moscow still treated Finland as the next target and opened fire on 30 November without a formal declaration of war. The League of Nations took the case up in December, and its investigation reported in March 1940 that the Soviet action amounted to aggression, but the Soviet Union had by then already been excluded from the activities of the League, and no sanctions could follow. The German factor mattered just as much: in the later 1930s Germany and Finland had close economic ties, and the trade in potash and nickel gave Germany access to Arctic resources, while Moscow read it as a channel for German expansion into Finland; secret agreements signed in 1939 between Berlin and Helsinki were not unknown to the Soviet Union. Moscow equally needed a victory, to show the West that its action was defensive in character and to consolidate the new order in eastern Europe. Finland had calculations of its own: neither the Defence Council nor the presidential office wanted the Communist Party to grow powerful during the war, and the Finnish party had been gaining ground rapidly before the war, a fact that entered Moscow's arithmetic as well.
impact: 冬季戰爭的結局扭轉了芬蘭的地緣位置，也決定了它此後半個世紀的外交取向。芬蘭失去卡累利阿地峽、拉多加卡累利阿、薩拉與佩察莫等大片土地，總面積約佔全國一成多，並交出漢科港的租借權；居住在被割讓地區的數萬名卡累利阿居民被迫遷移，被蘇軍佔領區的居民更被成批流放到白海與西伯亞的勞動營地，芬蘭社會此後十餘年都忙於安置這些移民。一九四〇年的和約並沒有帶來安寧：翌年德國進攻蘇聯，芬蘭以「共同戰線」的名義加入對蘇作戰，收復維堡等地，但一九四四年秋在蘇軍反攻與國內局勢的雙重擠壓下，不得不割讓大片領土、驅逐境內德軍，並簽訂對蘇和約；緊接而來的拉普蘭戰爭，使芬蘭人對德國的信任徹底破滅，也讓西歐國家相信芬蘭並非不可靠的盟友。一九四八年芬蘇簽訂友好合作互助條約，一九四七年巴黎和約已把佩察莫歸還芬蘭，一九五六年芬蘭再以讓出波爾卡拉一段土地作交換調整邊界。從軍事角度看，這場戰爭的效果更為直接：蘇聯在冬季戰爭中付出的人命、物資與時間遠超預期，卻只在芬蘭境內換得一條勉強守住的邊界，此後二十餘年蘇軍再未嘗試北進，直到一九四一年再次動手而更加失手；反觀芬蘭，冬季戰爭的經驗直接催生一九四〇年之後的國防改革，兵役期延長、冬季裝備與滑雪部隊制度化、堡壘與兵工生產的規模都因此擴大，芬蘭軍隊由一支冬季徵召的民軍，轉為以冬季消耗戰為前提的常備國防。戰後的蘇聯同樣要交學費：一九三八年的師制在這場戰爭中暴露大量問題，蘇軍此後改用新一型的編制、整頓冬季裝備，坦克與重砲集中使用的辦法亦在隨後數年重寫；而德芬之間的密切關係則在戰後被和約條文限制，芬蘭未經蘇聯同意不得向德國提供任何軍事或經濟援助，違者視為對蘇開戰，這一條在四年後芬蘭退出戰爭的過程中成為各方交涉的焦點。
impactEn: The outcome of the Winter War rearranged Finland's geopolitical position and fixed the direction of its foreign policy for the next half century. Finland lost the Karelian Isthmus, Ladoga Karelia, Salla and Petsamo, something over a tenth of its national territory, and surrendered the lease on the naval base at Hanko; tens of thousands of Karelians living in the ceded areas were uprooted, and the population of the occupied districts was deported in batches to labour camps around the White Sea and in Siberia, while Finnish society spent the following decade settling these migrants. The peace of 1940 brought no peace: the next year Germany attacked the Soviet Union, and Finland entered the war against the USSR under the banner of a common front, retaking Vyborg and other ground, but in the autumn of 1944, squeezed by the Soviet counter-offensive and by events at home, it had to cede territory, drive German troops out of the country and sign a separate peace with Moscow. The ensuing Lapland War destroyed Finnish confidence in Germany for good and convinced the Western powers that Finland was a reliable partner. A treaty of friendship, cooperation and mutual assistance was signed with the Soviet Union in 1948; Petsamo had already been returned to Finland under the Paris peace treaty of 1947, and in 1956 Finland adjusted the frontier once more by ceding a stretch of Porkkala on lease. The military consequences were even more direct. The Soviet Union had spent men, materiel and time far beyond its own expectations, and had bought in Finland only a frontier it could hold by force, and did not attempt to push north again for more than twenty years, until it struck in 1941 and fared even worse. The Finns, for their part, drew the lessons of the winter war straight into their defence reform: the length of military service was extended, winter equipment and ski troops were put on a systematic footing, and the scale of both fortifications and munitions production was enlarged. The Finnish army of 1940 was no longer a citizen levy called up for a winter, but a peacetime defence built on the premise of a war of attrition in the cold. The Soviet Union had its own lessons to draw: the 1938 establishment exposed many problems in this war, and the Red Army afterwards adopted a new divisional structure, reformed its winter equipment and rewrote the way it concentrated tanks and heavy artillery over the following years. The close German-Finnish relationship, meanwhile, was now constrained by the terms of the peace, which barred Finland from granting Germany any military or economic assistance without Soviet consent on pain of the treaty itself being treated as a casus belli, and that clause became the focus of the negotiations when Finland left the war four years later.
result: 四〇年三月十二日蘇聯與芬蘭在莫斯科簽訂和約，十三日批准，戰事就此結束。芬蘭保住了國土與主權，卻丟失了在戰前線的整條邊防地帶和比戰前更大的地盤。條約的主要內容包括：割讓卡累利阿地峽、拉多加卡累利阿、薩拉地區、佩察莫以及北方波羅的海的雷巴赫半島等土地；把漢科半島租給蘇聯三十年；芬軍撤出奧蘭群島並限制海軍與航空兵力的規模；以十四萬枚金幣分年支付戰爭賠償。結果是芬蘭被迫接受一條全新的國界，蘇軍得以把地峽前線縮回國境線上，列寧格勒與北方工業區的安全問題暫時解除，而蘇聯也自莫斯科和約中取得一項此前無法預期的收穫：芬蘭必須解散共產黨並切斷與西方的一切軍火交易，芬軍於同年春被縮編，許多團營被解散，國家機器轉向全面備戰。芬軍在戰役中展現的森林作戰、滑雪機動與堡壘防守，成為其後軍事研究與軍事外交的重要資本；戰俘問題上，蘇聯最終承認並遣返部分芬軍被俘人員，芬方則在戰後安置被遣返的軍人與家屬，兩國在四〇年二月已完成第一批俘虜的交換。芬蘭的國內政治亦因之改變：曼納海姆在四〇年三月當選總統，國防委員會的權力在戰後被削弱，議會與內閣的權力重新分配。和約亦明文限制芬蘭未經蘇聯同意不得向德國提供援助，違者視為對蘇開戰；雙方並在二月初已交換第一批俘虜，戰後芬蘭共產黨隨即解散，議會中的黨籍議員全部退黨，議會在三月二十六日批准和約。戰爭的終局也把兩國的戰後關係釘在一段長期對抗的起點上：和約簽訂後，芬蘭被迫在外交上靠攏莫斯科，莫斯科則以更高的姿態處理波羅的海事務；北極圈的爭端、奧蘭群島的軍備限制與佩察莫的租借，則在往後二十餘年成為兩國不斷重提的舊帳。
resultEn: On 12 March 1940 the Soviet Union and Finland signed a peace treaty in Moscow which was ratified the following day, and the fighting was over. Finland kept its territory and its sovereignty, but lost the entire belt of frontier defences it had held before the war and a larger stretch of ground than it had possessed beforehand. The main terms were the cession of the Karelian Isthmus, Ladoga Karelia, the Salla region, Petsamo and the Rybachy Peninsula in the northern Baltic; a thirty-year lease of the Hanko Peninsula to the Soviet Union; the withdrawal of Finnish troops from the Åland Islands and restrictions on the size of the Finnish navy and air force; and war reparations of 140,000 gold coins paid in instalments. Finland was thus made to accept a new border, the Soviet army pulled the front on the Karelian Isthmus back to the state line, and the security of Leningrad and the northern industrial belt was temporarily settled. Moscow also drew from the peace treaty a gain it could not have predicted: Finland had to disband the Communist Party and sever every channel of arms purchases from the West, while the Finnish army was cut back in the spring and many of its formations were dissolved, the state machine turning wholly towards war preparation. The forest fighting, ski mobility and field fortification demonstrated by the Finnish army became capital studied afterwards by military planners and diplomats. On prisoners, the Soviet Union eventually acknowledged and repatriated part of the Finnish POWs, and on the Finnish side the demobilised soldiers and their families were resettled; the first exchange of prisoners had in fact been completed in February 1940. Finnish domestic politics changed with the war as well: Mannerheim was elected president in March 1940, the authority of the Defence Council was reduced after the conflict, and power was redistributed between the parliament and the cabinet. The treaty likewise barred Finland from granting assistance to Germany without Soviet consent, on pain of being treated as a casus belli; the first prisoners were exchanged in the first days of February, the Finnish Communist Party was dissolved immediately after the war and all its members of parliament resigned, and the parliament ratified the treaty on 26 March. The end of the war also nailed the two countries into the opening phase of a long contest: after the treaty Finland was pushed diplomatically towards Moscow, while Moscow dealt with Baltic affairs from a position of greater confidence, and the Arctic frontier, the demilitarisation of the Åland Islands and the lease of Petsamo became old scores reopened again over the following twenty years.
